output.subject: Graph Data Structures and Algorithms
output.purpose: Interview preparation for a technical interview next month
output.target_capability: Recall and apply core graph algorithms (traversal, shortest path, MST, topological sort, cycle detection, etc.) and common patterns (BFS/DFS templates, union-find, Dijkstra, etc.) under interview time pressure
inferred: entry_point: no prior graph knowledge assumed; the cheat sheet must be self-contained
depth_register: concise reference format — definitions, complexities, template code snippets, and when-to-use cues; no proofs or extended derivations
template: none specified; a compact multi-page reference grouped by algorithm family

axes.would_differ: If the subject were 'tree DSA' or 'general DSA', the concept list would shift entirely — no graph-specific algorithms (Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, topological sort, SCC, flow) and different template code.

If the purpose were 'course exam' or 'competitive programming', the cheat sheet would include more theorems, proof sketches, and edge-case handling; for interviews it prioritizes recognising the pattern, writing clean code fast, and explaining time/space trade-offs.

A first-time learner needs definitions of graph representations, BFS/DFS intuition, and step-by-step trace examples; an experienced engineer needs only the templates, complexities, and common pitfalls. The concept set and depth per concept change drastically.
axes.reason: weak (unknown) and a different answer would change the plan

axes.value: Recall and apply core graph algorithms (traversal, shortest path, MST, topological sort, cycle detection, etc.) and common patterns (BFS/DFS templates, union-find, Dijkstra, etc.) under interview time pressure
axes.would_differ: If the target were 'explain graph theory concepts' or 'design graph systems', the artifact would shift from code templates + complexity tables to conceptual diagrams and architectural patterns.
If the capacity were 'one week', the cheat sheet would be ultra-condensed (top 10 patterns only); if 'three months', it could include practice problem maps and spaced-repetition cues.
axes.reason: never asked — Semantics §1 LOCKED — optional, and the corollary: deriving the plan and reporting its extent is what CAUSES a capacity to be stated. Asking upfront asks for a number the learner cannot honestly give.

axes.would_differ: A 'deep' register would include correctness invariants, proof sketches, and variant analyses; a 'shallow' register would be only one-liner signatures and complexities. The page count and cognitive load differ by 3–5×.
axes.reason: never asked — Semantics §1 — biasing, not binding. A default is always defensible.

axes.would_differ: If the artifact were 'detailed notes', each algorithm would get a full section with intuition, walkthrough, variants, and 2–3 solved examples; a 'flashcard deck' would be atomic Q/A pairs. The structure and information density are fundamentally different.

A 'language-specific' template (e.g., Python-only with collections.deque) would omit C++/Java equivalents; a 'pattern-first' template would group by BFS/DFS/DP-on-graphs rather than by algorithm name. The partitioning of the cheat sheet changes.

concepts.name: Number of Islands / Connected Components in Grid
Cheapest Flights Within K Stops / Bellman-Ford Application

judgements.why: Fundamental; every graph problem starts with choosing a representation. Adjacency list is the default for sparse graphs in interviews.
Needed for dense graphs, Floyd-Warshall, and problems where O(1) edge lookup matters. Interviewers expect candidates to discuss tradeoffs.
Required for Kruskal's and Bellman-Ford; also appears in union-find problems. Compact and worth a one-line note.
Core traversal; basis for shortest path in unweighted graphs, topological sort (Kahn's), multi-source BFS, and grid problems. Must have template.
Core traversal; basis for cycle detection (directed), topological sort (DFS), SCC, and backtracking. Recursive template is standard.
Avoids recursion depth limits; explicit stack control. Interviewers sometimes ask for iterative version. Distinct template.
Directly tested (Number of Islands, provinces); also underpins union-find use cases. Template applies to grids and explicit graphs.
Common interview question (redundant connection, valid tree). Two standard approaches: DFS with parent tracking, and Union-Find.
Course schedule, alien dictionary, deadlock detection. Uses three-color DFS or Kahn's indegree check. Distinct from undirected.
Appears as standalone question (is graph bipartite?) and as subroutine in matching. BFS/DFS coloring template is short and high-yield.
Most common topological sort in interviews (Course Schedule I/II). Intuitive, handles cycle detection naturally. Must have template.
Alternative approach; useful when post-order logic is needed (e.g., Alien Dictionary with lexicographic order). Good to know both.
Foundation for grid/maze shortest path, multi-source BFS, and 0-1 BFS. Simpler than Dijkstra; often sufficient.
Single-source shortest path with non-negative weights. High-frequency interview topic (Network Delay Time, Cheapest Flights variants). Template essential.
Handles negative weights and detects negative cycles. Cheapest Flights Within K Stops is a classic constrained variant. Template worth including.
All-pairs shortest path; O(V^3). Appears in 'minimum score of path between two cities' type problems. Small template, high signal.
Heuristic search; rare in general SWE interviews. More relevant for game dev or robotics roles. Cut for capacity.
MST with dense graphs or when starting from a node. Similar structure to Dijkstra; good to contrast. Connecting cities, min cost to connect all points.
MST with sparse graphs; relies on Union-Find. Classic interview problem (connect all points, optimizing edges). Must know Union-Find first.
Standalone data structure; powers Kruskal, cycle detection (undirected), dynamic connectivity (Accounts Merge, Redundant Connection). Path compression + union by rank template is mandatory.
SCC is advanced; Kosaraju/Tarjan rarely appear in general interviews. Only for hard graph-specific roles. Cut for capacity.
Same as Kosaraju; single-pass but more complex. Not expected in standard interview loop.
Cheat sheet must have copy-pasteable template: queue, visited, level-order loop. Highest ROI for interview recall.
Standard recursive pattern with visited set. Used for components, cycle detection, topological sort, backtracking.
Explicit stack version; avoids recursion limit. Some interviewers prefer it. Compact enough to include both.
Priority queue + distance map + relaxation. Variations: early exit, path reconstruction. Must-have template.
Find with path compression, union by rank/size. Used in 5+ common problems. One of the highest-value templates.
Both Kahn's (queue + indegree) and DFS (post-order reverse). Cheat sheet should show both side-by-side with when-to-use.
Most graph problems in interviews are on grids (islands, walls, rotting oranges). Directions array + bounds check pattern is distinct and essential.
Rotting Oranges, Walls and Gates, 01 Matrix. Initialize queue with all sources. High-frequency pattern, one-line modification of BFS template.
Shortest path with 0/1 edge weights (e.g., minimum obstacles removal). Deque instead of priority queue. Niche but appears in top-tier interviews; small template.
Clone Graph (LeetCode 133) is a classic. Uses BFS/DFS + hash map. Demonstrates handling cycles in graph copying. Worth a snippet.
Canonical topological sort + cycle detection problem. Course Schedule I (bool), II (ordering), IV (queries). Must-recognize pattern.

judgements.concept: Number of Islands / Connected Components in Grid
judgements.why: Most common grid graph problem. Tests BFS/DFS on implicit graph, visited marking, directions. Template directly reusable.
BFS on grid with distance tracking. Nearest Exit, Shortest Path in Binary Matrix. Direct application of unweighted shortest path.
Standard Dijkstra problem: single-source, weighted, find max distance. Also tests priority queue usage and unreachable nodes.

judgements.concept: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops / Bellman-Ford Application
judgements.why: Constrained shortest path (exactly K edges / at most K stops). Bellman-Ford or modified Dijkstra. High-signal variant.
Find edge that creates cycle in undirected graph. Direct Union-Find application. Also solvable with DFS. Classic.
Union-Find on strings (emails) with mapping to indices. Merges components, then collects. Tests DSU + hash map composition.
Build graph from word list, then topological sort. Tests graph construction + ordering. Hard but famous; good to have cue.
Hierholzer's algorithm / post-order DFS. Lexicographic order constraint. Appears in top-tier interviews (Google, Meta). Compact template.
Advanced; only for specialized roles (quant, infra, hard graph teams). Not in general SWE interview bar. Cut.
Advanced matching algorithm. Rarely asked directly; maximum bipartite matching sometimes appears but usually reduced to flow. Cut.

sequence: Graph DSA Cheat Sheet for Interviews
output.why: Single coherent subject — a cheat sheet is one document the learner studies in one sitting. All concepts are reference material for the same job (retrieve under interview pressure); splitting would fragment the lookup surface.

exclusions.consequence: Cannot solve heuristic-guided pathfinding problems (e.g., game AI, robotics motion planning) if they appear; will default to Dijkstra and lose efficiency.
exclusions.when_to_learn: When targeting game dev, robotics, or specialized pathfinding roles — after mastering Dijkstra.

exclusions.consequence: Cannot decompose directed graphs into SCCs in linear time; will miss problems requiring condensation DAG (e.g., 2-SAT, capital city problems).
exclusions.when_to_learn: If a hard graph-specific interview asks for SCC explicitly, or when studying advanced algorithms (competitive programming, distributed systems).

exclusions.consequence: Same as Kosaraju — cannot produce SCCs in one DFS pass; loses the low-link optimization that some interviewers probe for.
exclusions.when_to_learn: Same as Kosaraju; Tarjan is the single-pass alternative sometimes requested in follow-up.

exclusions.consequence: Cannot solve max-flow / min-cut problems (bipartite matching via flow, network reliability, image segmentation); will not recognize the reduction pattern.
exclusions.when_to_learn: Quant, infrastructure, or hard graph-team interviews; after mastering BFS and residual graphs.

exclusions.consequence: Cannot solve maximum bipartite matching in O(E√V); will fall back to slower DFS augmenting paths or max-flow reduction and risk TLE.
exclusions.when_to_learn: Competitive programming or when matching appears as a standalone hard problem; after understanding bipartite check and max-flow.

MST for dense graphs or node-start. Priority queue similar to Dijkstra. Connecting cities, min cost to connect all points. Contrast with Kruskal.
MST for sparse graphs; relies on Union-Find. Sort edges + union. Classic interview problem. Must know Union-Find first.
Standalone data structure powering Kruskal, cycle detection (undirected), dynamic connectivity. Path compression + union by rank template is mandatory.
Copy-pasteable template: queue, visited, level-order loop. Highest ROI for interview recall. Must show generic structure + grid adaptation.
Standard recursive pattern with visited set. Used for components, cycle detection, topological sort, backtracking. Generic + grid variants.
Explicit stack version; avoids recursion limit. Some interviewers prefer it. Compact enough to include both.
Priority queue + distance map + relaxation. Variations: early exit, path reconstruction. Must-have template for weighted graphs.
Find with path compression, union by rank/size. Used in 5+ common problems. One of the highest-value templates.
Both Kahn's (queue + indegree) and DFS (post-order reverse) side-by-side with when-to-use cues. Directly copy-pasteable.
Most interview graph problems are on grids. Directions array + bounds check + visited marking pattern is distinct and essential.
Rotting Oranges, Walls and Gates, 01 Matrix. Initialize queue with all sources. One-line modification of BFS template. High-frequency.
Shortest path with 0/1 edge weights (min obstacles removal). Deque instead of PQ. Niche but appears in top-tier interviews; small template.
Clone Graph (LeetCode 133) classic. BFS/DFS + hash map (old→new). Demonstrates handling cycles in copying. Worth a snippet.

modules.why_here: All concepts serve the single job: a compact reference the learner keeps open during interview prep and recalls under time pressure. Every item is a lookup target (definition, complexity, template, or problem→algorithm mapping) for the same domain. Splitting would force the learner to switch PDFs mid-lookup.
modules.capability: Look up and apply any core graph algorithm, traversal template, or canonical problem pattern needed in a technical interview — including choosing the right representation, writing BFS/DFS/Dijkstra/Union-Find/Topological Sort from memory, and recognizing which template fits a new problem.
